# Cūḷavedalla Sutta (MN 44 (PTS MN i 299))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷavedalla Sutta* (MN 44), also referred to as the *Dhammadinnā Sutta*, is an important doctrinal discourse set in Rājagaha [Klaus & Hartmann 2007; Bingenheimer 2006]. In this sutta, the layman Visākha questions the arahant nun Dhammadinnā—traditionally identified as his former wife—on subtle points of doctrine and high meditative attainments, culminating in the Buddha fully endorsing her explanations [Analayo 2014; Skilling 2001]. Although framed in a technical question-and-answer format, the exchange represents early discourse rather than formal Abhidharma [Analayo 2014].

The discussion covers the definition of identity (*sakkāya*), its arising, and its cessation; the Noble Eightfold Path and its distribution into the three aggregates (*khandha*), placing right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration within the concentration aggregate (*samādhikkhandha*); and the nature of concentration (*samādhi*), defined as unification of the mind (*cittassa ekaggatā*) with the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) as its condition or basis (*samādhinimitta*) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Wen 2011]. Dhammadinnā also details the conditioned nature of feelings (*vedanā*), distinguishing commendable pleasant feelings from those leading to unwholesome reactions, and defines bodily activity (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) as in- and out-breathing and mental activity (*cittasaṅkhāra*) as feeling and perception, in the context of gradual cessation leading to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) [Analayo 2014; Analayo 2019; Buswell & Lopez 2014].

Curated parallels include Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* discourse MĀ 210 (*Fale biqiuni jing*), a citation in Śamathadeva’s *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* (Up 1.005), as well as parallels in the Saṁyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāyas (SN 22.44, SN 41.3, SN 41.6, SĀ 568, AN 4.200) and the *Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta* (MN 109) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Skilling 2001]. While the Pāli version is set in Rājagaha with the male disciple Visākha, its Chinese counterpart in MĀ situates the discourse at Sāvatthī, apparently confusing him with the female disciple Visākhā, and reverses the sequence of the *Cūḷavedalla* and *Mahāvedalla* suttas while exchanging certain questions between them [Klaus & Hartmann 2007]. Automated text-reuse data from DharmaNexus confirms major cross-canonical parallels with SN 22, SN 41, SN 36, and MN 109, as well as alignment with Sanskrit works like the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* and Tibetan translations [DharmaNexus].
